clue.text: Change poles for entry into 11

indicators.note: making an entry into something means going inside it, so these pieces go within the vehicle

blocks.note: the north and south poles, abbreviated
taken as written
the answer to 11 is a streetcar, which in Britain is a tram

explanation.surface: Someone swaps the trolley poles to get onto a streetcar.
explanation.walkthrough: The cross-reference is not used as written: 11 is a streetcar, and you need the British word for one before anything can go inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: To transform something is to alter its form completely, a straightforward synonym of the verb.

clue.text: 3's charm

definitions.note: a work by 3, Sir Walter Scott

blocks.note: first meaning: a novel by the writer at 3-down
second meaning: an object believed to bring luck or protection

explanation.walkthrough: This puzzle has a theme of Scott's works; The Talisman is his 1825 novel set during the Crusades.
explanation.definitionFit: A talisman is an amulet or lucky object, and The Talisman is also one of Scott's crusading novels.

clue.text: The nurse from hell?

blocks.note: surface reading: a monstrous, cruel nurse
setter's reading: a kindly nurse is often called this, and the Hell's motorcycle gang shares the name

explanation.walkthrough: A devoted nurse is called an angel, and the motorcycle gang called Hell's Angels make an angel one who comes from hell.
explanation.definitionFit: A gentle, caring nurse is affectionately called an angel, and a member of the Hell's biker club is one too.

clue.text: Writer's writ's changed - changes bed inside

indicators.note: something changed has been altered, so these letters are put in a new order
inside tells us the following pieces sit within the jumbled letters

blocks.note: the letters of writ's, rearranged
changes as a verb, a simple synonym
a cot is a small bed

explanation.surface: A writer's legal document has been altered, with a bed tucked inside.
explanation.walkthrough: The word 'changes' does double service in the surface, but here it is a plain synonym; only 'changed' signals the jumble. Note the jumble's last letter stays outside the inserted pair.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Walter Scott was the Scottish novelist and poet, author of Ivanhoe and the Waverley novels.

clue.text: Farm offices in Scotland sound the opposite of the schools regulator

indicators.note: sound tells us to go by how a phrase is spoken, not how it is spelt

blocks.clueFragment: the opposite of the schools regulator
blocks.note: Ofsted, the English schools inspectorate, sounds like off-sted; its opposite would be on-sted

explanation.surface: A puzzling description of Scottish farm buildings that somehow involves school inspectors.
explanation.walkthrough: Ofsted is the body that inspects schools in England; swapping its 'off' for 'on' gives a sound matching this Scots word.
explanation.definitionFit: Onstead is a Scottish dialect word for a farmstead, the farmhouse together with its outbuildings.

clue.text: 3's girl eating her head

definitions.note: a work by 3, Sir Walter Scott

indicators.note: a head is the top, so we keep just the opening letter of her name
eating means taking something inside, so the girl swallows the other piece

blocks.note: a girl's name
her refers back to the girl, so it is the first letter of her name

explanation.surface: A girl from Scott's story devouring her own head, a gruesome image.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Her' points back to the girl, so the letter swallowed is her own initial. Marmion is Scott's 1808 narrative poem about the Battle of Flodden.
explanation.definitionFit: Marmion is the long narrative poem by Scott, so it is a work belonging to the writer at 3.

clue.text: That is nearly the date

indicators.note: nearly means not quite all, so the last letter is dropped

blocks.note: id est is the Latin for that is, abbreviated i.e.

explanation.surface: Someone says that it is nearly the right day.
explanation.walkthrough: Drop the final T from ID EST. The Ides was a specific Roman calendar day, the 15th or 13th of the month.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Roman calendar the Ides is a particular day of each month, famously in March.

clue.text: Church official a fairy, reportedly: relax constraint

indicators.note: reportedly means as it is spoken, so we want the sound of the phrase

blocks.note: a deacon is a church official and a troll is a creature of folklore

explanation.surface: A churchman is rumoured to be a fairy; meanwhile someone loosens the rules.
explanation.walkthrough: A troll is a supernatural being from Scandinavian folklore, loosely a fairy.
explanation.definitionFit: To decontrol is to remove official controls or restrictions, which is relaxing a constraint.

clue.text: See 18
Agent dealing with gift to take up musical

indicators.note: in a down entry taking up means lifting the word so it reads from the bottom upwards

blocks.note: re means concerning or about
a present is a gift
the Lloyd Webber musical about Eva Perón

explanation.surface: An agent handles a gift meant to promote a stage musical.
explanation.walkthrough: EVITA is read upwards to give ATIVE, completing RE + PRESENT + ATIVE.
explanation.definitionFit: A representative acts for someone else, which is what an agent does.

clue.text: The drink of kings from the right

indicators.note: reading from the right means starting at the end of the word and going backwards

blocks.note: regal means belonging to or fit for kings

explanation.surface: A beverage favoured by monarchs, served from the right-hand side.
explanation.definitionFit: Lager is a light beer, the everyday drink in many pubs.

clue.text: Desire the way back and the rest will be included

definitions.note: the streetcar named Desire, in Tennessee Williams's play

indicators.note: something included is placed inside, so this piece goes within another

blocks.note: ST is the abbreviation for street, a way
the rear is the back
etc. stands for et cetera, and the rest

explanation.surface: A wish to go back, with everything else to be packed in too.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Desire' is a proper name, not a feeling: it is the vehicle in Tennessee Williams's A Streetcar Named Desire. The abbreviation for the rest sits within the word for back.
explanation.definitionFit: In Tennessee Williams's play, Desire is the name of a New Orleans tram route, so Desire is one.

clue.text: Opposed to silver being put in auction - rescue needed

indicators.note: being put in something means placed inside it, so these pieces sit within the other

blocks.note: an auction is a type of sale
v. for versus, against
Ag is the chemical symbol for silver

explanation.surface: Someone against selling the family silver at auction calls for a rescue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Opposed to' gives the single letter used in sports fixtures, as in Arsenal v Spurs.
explanation.definitionFit: Salvage means saving goods or a ship from loss or wreckage, a recovery operation.

clue.text: Not too far for Grannie, possibly

indicators.note: possibly suggests one of several arrangements, so the name's letters may be shuffled

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A trip that is manageable for an elderly grandmother, perhaps.
explanation.definitionFit: Something in range is within reach, close enough to hit or get to, so not too distant.

clue.text: Poseur requiring aid? It isn't true

indicators.note: requiring help implies the letters need putting right, so they are rearranged

blocks.note: every letter of this phrase, apostrophe and question mark ignored

explanation.surface: A show-off asks for help, and someone retorts that his act is false.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole of 'aid? It isn't true' is the fodder; the phrase 'isn't true' also hints that the letters are not in their true order.
explanation.definitionFit: An attitudiniser strikes affected attitudes for effect, which is exactly what a poseur does.

clue.text: Superior woodcutter gets a penny for a mile from Twain character

indicators.note: for here means in place of, so one letter replaces another

blocks.note: p is the abbreviation for a penny
m is the abbreviation for a mile
the boy hero of Mark Twain's novel

explanation.surface: A skilled lumberjack is given a coin to replace a mile in Twain's story.
explanation.walkthrough: Swap the M in TOM SAWYER for P. In a sawpit the top sawyer stood above the log and was the senior partner.
explanation.definitionFit: The top sawyer worked the upper end of a pit saw, the senior position, hence also a person of high standing.

clue.text: 3's station on  ...

definitions.note: a work by 3, Sir Walter Scott

blocks.note: first meaning: Scott's first novel, which gave its name to the whole series
second meaning: the main railway station in Edinburgh

explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis runs on into 18-down: Edinburgh's main station stands at the foot of Princes Street, and was named after Scott's novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Waverley is Scott's 1814 novel and also the name of Edinburgh's principal railway terminus.

clue.text: Standard first page has Gore in rupture with the trappings

indicators.note: in here places the named politician inside the injury

blocks.note: par is the standard or norm
A as in A1, first-class
p is the abbreviation for page
a hernia is commonly called a rupture
Al Gore, the US vice-president

explanation.surface: A front-page report about Al Gore's injury, complete with all the trimmings.
explanation.walkthrough: Gore is Al Gore, who had just lost the 2000 US presidential election when this appeared; 'first' as A comes from A1, first-rate.
explanation.definitionFit: Paraphernalia are miscellaneous belongings or equipment, the accessories and trappings of an activity.

clue.text: ...  sewage plant in reproduction

definitions.note: the ellipsis continues 16: the street that Waverley station is on

indicators.note: in places the first pieces inside the copy

blocks.note: a print is a reproduction of a picture
cess is an old word for sewage, as in cesspit
a tree is a plant

explanation.surface: Waverley station sits beside a waste-treatment works in a copy of something.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer runs across 18 and 8, and the ellipsis carries on from 16. Princes Street is Edinburgh's main shopping street; cess is an old word for sewage.
explanation.definitionFit: Edinburgh's Waverley station lies just below Princes Street, so the street is where the station is found.

clue.text: Old navigator giving coiners trouble

indicators.note: something given trouble is disturbed, so its letters are thrown into disorder

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A sailor of old makes life difficult for forgers.
explanation.definitionFit: Leif Ericson was the Norse explorer who sailed to North America around the year 1000.

clue.text: Waters part for modest heroine

definitions.note: the heroine of George Moore's novel Esther Waters

indicators.note: part means only a portion of the following words is used

blocks.note: found running across these two words

explanation.surface: An actress takes a role as a demure female lead.
explanation.walkthrough: Esther Waters, George Moore's 1894 novel, is about a modest servant girl; her surname is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Esther is the first name of the character surnamed Waters, the title heroine of Moore's novel.

clue.text: Advertiser gives his cat a cuckoo

indicators.note: cuckoo means crazy, so the letters go mad and are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An ad man hands his pet cat a bird.
explanation.definitionFit: Saatchi & Saatchi is the famous British advertising agency founded by the Saatchi brothers.

clue.text: 3's house, one with wind indicator outside

definitions.note: a work by 3, Sir Walter Scott

indicators.note: outside means one piece wraps around another

blocks.note: the Roman numeral for one
a weather vane shows wind direction
ho. is the abbreviation for house

explanation.surface: Scott's house has a weathervane on the outside.
explanation.walkthrough: '3's house' looks like the definition, but 'house' belongs to the wordplay; the definition is just '3's', one of Scott's novels.
explanation.definitionFit: Ivanhoe is Scott's 1819 novel of Saxons and Normans, so it is one of the works of 3.

clue.text: Astronomy ends in something black, according to this expert

indicators.note: ends picks out the last letter of the word before it
in places that letter inside the black thing

blocks.note: the final letter of the word
a black hole, in astronomy

explanation.surface: Astronomy ends up inside a black hole, says an authority on the subject.
explanation.walkthrough: 'According to Hoyle' means by the rules, after Edmond Hoyle, the authority on card games; Fred Hoyle was also an astronomer.
explanation.definitionFit: Edmond Hoyle wrote the standard rulebooks on whist and other games, so he is the expert in the idiom.

clue.text: Needle covers in the ring?

blocks.note: surface reading: sheaths for sewing needles, perhaps in a sewing ring
setter's reading: what hides a needle in the proverb, and the name of a famous wrestler

explanation.walkthrough: Looking for a needle in a haystack is proverbially hopeless; Giant Haystacks was a huge British TV wrestler of the 1970s and 80s.
explanation.definitionFit: Stacks of hay proverbially hide needles, and Giant Haystacks fought in the wrestling ring.

clue.text: Poem to the beautiful Lydia partly returned

indicators.note: partly means only a portion of the phrase is taken
returned means sent back, so the letters are read in the opposite direction

blocks.note: the letters spanning the two words

explanation.surface: A love poem written to a lovely woman called Lydia, sent back to the poet.
explanation.definitionFit: An idyll is a short poem describing an idealised pastoral scene.

clue.text: Remarkably pink?

blocks.note: first meaning: an old-fashioned intensifier
second meaning: of meat, lightly cooked

explanation.walkthrough: As an adverb the word means exceptionally, as in 'a rare fine day'; steak that is still pink inside is underdone.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is an informal intensifier meaning exceptionally, and describes meat cooked so it stays pink.

clue.text: Afterwards trust and yours may come first

definitions.note: describes the letter sign-off in which it is preceded by yours

blocks.note: since can mean afterwards, as in 'I have not seen him since'
to rely on is to trust

explanation.surface: A note on trusting later, signed off with a closing phrase.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a description: the word that follows 'Yours' at the end of a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Letters conventionally end 'Yours sincerely', so the possessive pronoun sits before this adverb.
